findings.headline: HRA Business Plan under review with development milestones deferred to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has commissioned a review of its HRA (Housing Revenue Account) Business Plan. As a result, the draft housing development pipeline report did not go to Cabinet in January 2026 and the revised Blackshots redevelopment business case is now subject to the outcome of this review. Both are reprofiled into 2026/27.
findings.matters: A decision to review the HRA Business Plan may signal financial stress on the housing revenue account or discovery of issues requiring reassessment. Deferrals of housing development projects reduce capital investment and could impact housing supply plans.
findings.figures: Cabinet report deferred from January 2026; Blackshots business case review linked to HRA outcome
findings.quote: The cabinet report did not go to January 2026 Cabinet due to recently commissioned review of HRA Business Plan. This will be reprofiled in 2026/27 in line with HRA Business Plan review outcome… The business case for redevelopment is subject to a full review of the HRA Business Plan to be completed in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Public Sector Internal Audit Standards compliance below 75% with action plan delayed to Q2 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has not met its target of 75% compliance with Public Sector Internal Audit Standards (PSIAS). Gaps have been identified and an action plan is being produced for presentation to the Audit Committee in Q2 of 2026/27. In parallel, a Finance Improvement Plan is being aligned to strengthen internal controls and governance.
findings.matters: Audit standard gaps and the existence of a separate Finance Improvement Plan suggest internal control weaknesses. For a lender, audit and governance deficiencies directly affect credit assessment and the council's ability to detect and prevent financial issues.
findings.figures: Below 75% compliance target; action plan delivery in Q2 2026/27
findings.quote: While work has progressed, gaps have been identified against the standards, resulting in below 75% compliance. An action plan is being produced to address the gaps identified, which will be presented to both SLT and the Audit Committee in Q2 of 2026/27.

findings.headline: Agency staff spending 63% above budget at £16.3m, though improving
findings.detail: End-of-year spend on agency staff reached £16.3m against a target of £10m—an overspend of £6.3m. Whilst the paper notes positive progress in reducing reliance on agency workers in Q4 and successful permanent conversions, the council plans to continue recruiting agency staff for Local Government Reorganisation work, which is described as the most appropriate approach.
findings.matters: A £6.3m agency overspend indicates staffing volatility and cost control challenges. While the trajectory is improving, the council's decision to use agency for LGR work signals anticipated medium-term staffing uncertainty.
findings.figures: Actual £15.7m–£16.3m against target £10m (63% overspend); last year £4.4m
findings.quote: Spend on agency staff £16.3 million [Target] £10 million… posts supporting LGR activity will continue to be recruited on an agency basis, as this remains the most appropriate and flexible approach to secure the capacity and specialist capability required to deliver this work.

findings.headline: Children's external placement costs sustained at 13% above budget amid rising complexity
findings.detail: The average weekly cost of external placements for looked-after children reached £2,912 in Q4, compared to the target of £2,583—an overspend of £329 per week. The paper attributes this to structural increases in the complexity of needs requiring higher-cost care packages. This represents a material and sustained cost pressure beyond the council's direct control.
findings.matters: This is not a temporary overspend but a structural cost pressure driven by demand complexity. For a lender, sustained cost growth in a demand-led budget line signals tightening financial flexibility, particularly if future increases are expected.
findings.figures: Q4 average £2,912 per week vs budget £2,583 (13% overspend); compared to £2,500 in the previous year
findings.quote: The overall needs of children in Thurrock's care continue to increase, resulting in a sustained requirement for higher-cost care packages. This pressure is reflected in the Q4 average placement cost, which has remained high at £2,912, compared with £2,500 in the previous year, demonstrating the ongoing financial impact of increasing complexity.

findings.headline: Asset disposal plan delivering less than one-third of target and major receipts reprofiled
findings.detail: The council planned to realise £6.175m from asset disposals but delivered only £1.752m, a shortfall of £4.373m. Beyond this, significant transactions totalling approximately £40m have been reprofiled into future financial years. The shortfall stems from non-realisation of planned receipts from specific assets including Safe as Houses, PWE, and lower proceeds than anticipated from TEO and the Shard investment.
findings.matters: Asset disposals are typically a key component of council financing plans and borrowing assumptions. A £4.4m shortfall plus £40m in delayed receipts signals cash-flow pressure and potential implications for the council's medium-term financial strategy.
findings.figures: Delivered £1.752m against budget £6.175m (28% outturn); £40m of significant transactions reprofiled to future years
findings.quote: Divestments have delivered £1.752m against a budget of £6.175m, resulting in a shortfall of £4.373m. This reflects the non-realisation of planned receipts from specific assets, including Safe as Houses and PWE, together with lower than anticipated proceeds from TEO and the Shard investment. In addition, significant transactions with an estimated combined value of £40m have been reprofiled and are now expected in future financial years.

findings.headline: £7.4m of education Basic Needs grant remains unallocated to specific projects
findings.detail: Thurrock holds £7.4m of Government Basic Needs funding for primary and secondary education that 'remains uncommitted to specific projects at this time'. The council is conducting 'ongoing engagement with schools' to identify expansion strategies but has not yet allocated the funding.
findings.matters: Education capacity planning may not be complete; significant grant funding sits undeployed while schools engagement continues.

findings.quote: The allocation of Governments Basic Needs funding for primary and secondary education remains uncommitted to specific projects at this time. findings.headline: Thames Freeport required emergency MHCLG intervention to extend completion deadlines
findings.detail: Thames Freeport Seed Fund experienced delays serious enough to prompt MHCLG to grant 'freedoms and flexibilities' on 30 October 2025. Revised completion dates were extended, with most projects now expected by 31 July 2026 and remainder by 30 September 2026.
findings.matters: Major economic development scheme needed government-level intervention; indicates delivery capability and timeline problems.

findings.quote: The Thames Freeport Seed Fund programme has experienced delays in delivery; however, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) granted freedoms and flexibilities on 30 October 2025 to support qualifying projects in managing revised timescales.

findings.detail: The Local Authority Housing Fund project was ended because the second-stage tender 'produced a cost that exceeded the funding'. Thurrock is in discussions with MHCLG for resolution and would require a grant extension if an alternative delivery option is agreed.

findings.detail: Blackshots housing development has been entirely withdrawn following a viability review. Only £2.8m of budget is being carried forward, but for demolition costs rather than new housing delivery. A Cabinet paper is scheduled for July 2026 to establish the demolition budget.

findings.matters: School capacity project significantly behind schedule; impacts education provision and raises procurement risk questions.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care and Children's Services demographic pressures explicitly foreseen; new £1.5m reserve created December 2024

The council simultaneously created three additional children's services reserves: Supporting Families (£0.291m), Families First Partnership (£0.423m), and youth remand costs (£0.156m), all new in 2025/26.
findings.matters: The council has identified specific anticipated demands in social care that it cannot absorb within baseline budgets and is earmarking resources ahead of time. The forward reserve creation signals known pressures, not routine variance.

findings.headline: Capital program delivered at 27% of budget; £82m of £120m slipped to future years
findings.detail: The council budgeted £120.25m for general fund capital expenditure in 2025/26 but delivered only £32.79m. The variance of £87.46m comprises £82.05m in actual slippage (projects deferred to following years) and £5.41m in schemes releasing funding. findings.matters: Material capital slippage indicates project delivery, resourcing, or planning constraints and defers borrowing requirements and debt servicing to future financial years, affecting the council's cash position and borrowing profile.

findings.headline: HRA Repairs & Maintenance overspent by £1.178m due to backlog and Awaab's Law compliance costs
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account reported a breakeven position with £1.702m added to reserves, but within that, Repairs & Maintenance overspent by £1.178m. The paper cites 'a backlog of works, higher void repair costs, and additional activity to meet compliance requirements, including Awaab's Law' as drivers. Awaab's Law (relating to damp and mould in social housing) creates a new regulatory compliance obligation. While Supervision & Management underspent by £1.174m (largely from vacancies and insurance recoveries), the repairs overspend is the underlying operational pressure.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance backlogs are costly to clear and Awaab's Law creates an unfunded compliance obligation for social landlords. The HRA cannot simply avoid these costs — they are regulatory or safety-driven. This signals future HRA budget pressure and may limit flexibility to support the General Fund through HRA contributions.
findings.figures: HRA Repairs & Maintenance overspend £1.178m; driven by backlog of works, void repair costs, and Awaab's Law compliance
findings.quote: Repairs and Maintenance: The service reports an overspend of £1.178m, an increase of £0.486m from Quarter 3. This is primarily due to a backlog of works, higher void repair costs, and additional activity to meet compliance requirements, including Awaab's Law.

findings.headline: Divestment receipts fell £4.373m short of budget, with £40m of major transactions now pushed into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council budgeted £6.175m in divestment receipts for 2025/26 but received only £1.752m (71% shortfall). Key drivers: Safe as Houses contributed £0m (budget £3.0m), PWE contributed £0m (budget £0.8m), and TEO underperformed (£0.469m actual vs £1.0m budget). Critically, 'significant transactions with an estimated combined value of £40m, originally expected in late 2024/25 and reprofiled into 2025/26 will now be achieved in 2026/27'. Additionally, the forecast for total divestment receipts to 2028/29 has been reduced by £3.55m from previous assumptions due to 'updated expectations of market conditions'. The paper notes these are being used to reduce the council's Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.matters: Divestment delays and revised downward forecasts signal the council's asset disposal programme is not executing as expected and market conditions are tightening. If receipts are being counted on to reduce borrowing and capital financing costs, delays mean higher future borrowing costs and cash flow tightening. The £40m push into 2026/27 is a material refinancing risk.
findings.figures: 2025/26 divestment budget £6.175m, actual £1.752m (variance £4.373m adverse); Safe as Houses £0m vs £3.0m budget; PWE £0m vs £0.8m budget; TEO £0.469m vs £1.0m budget; £40m of transactions moved from 24/25/early 2025/26 into 2026/27; forecast to 2028/29 reduced by £3.55m from prior assumptions
findings.quote: Actual receipts were £1.752m, resulting in an adverse variance of £4.373m. This is mainly due to delays in asset disposals (including Safe as Houses and PWE), lower-than-expected receipts from TEO... In addition, significant transactions with an estimated combined value of £40m, originally expected in late 2024/25 and reprofiled into 2025/26 will now be achieved in 2026/27... The forecast for total receipts to 2028/29 is £100.55m, a reduction of £3.55m from previous assumptions, reflecting updated expectations of market conditions.

findings.headline: Finance directorate relies on £1.500m of agency staffing overspend to maintain statutory functions — flagged as structural pressure requiring action
findings.detail: The Finance Directorate overspent by £0.724m in 2025/26, but the core issue is structural: Corporate Finance recorded a £1.033m overspend driven 'primarily by significant agency staffing pressures of £1.500m, reflecting the requirement to maintain statutory and operational delivery'. This overspend is only partially offset by underspends on permanent staff vacancies. The directorate's MTFS commentary (section 7.19) explicitly states: 'These issues remain ongoing and are reflected within the Medium Term Financial Strategy. Actions are required to reduce dependency on agency resources, deliver sustainable workforce solutions'. This signals the council cannot currently attract or retain permanent staff in core finance roles.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on agency staff to deliver statutory finance functions (payroll, ledger, treasury) signals either market-driven wage pressure (indicating the council is uncompetitive) or structural vacancy (indicating capacity/culture issues). Statutory finance functions cannot be outsourced or cut; the council is paying a premium to keep them staffed. This is a run-rate cost pressure.
findings.figures: Finance Directorate overspend £0.724m; Corporate Finance overspend £1.033m; agency staffing overspend within Corporate Finance £1.500m; permanent staffing underspends partially offset this but do not eliminate it
findings.quote: significant agency staffing pressures of £1.500m, reflecting the requirement to maintain statutory and operational delivery... Actions are required to reduce dependency on agency resources, deliver sustainable workforce solutions and review cost recovery and income assumptions to ensure long-term financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Children's services placement costs are rising despite numbers being below budget, indicating complexity-driven cost inflation
findings.detail: Non-DSG Children's Services reported an underspend of only £0.008m in 2025/26, but this masks significant demand pressures. Placements and Support overspent by £1.151m while the actual number of placements (259) remained below the budget assumption of 275. This means each placement is costing more: external residential placements cost £14.564m for 27 placements (budget £11.405m for 27), and supported accommodation cost £1.574m for 20 placements (budget £1.038m for 16). The paper explicitly states costs are 'increasing due to greater complexity of need and higher support packages'. Additionally, No Recourse to Public Funds (NRPF) overspent by £0.707m — a statutory pressure where the council must house homeless families with dependent children.
findings.matters: Rising unit costs per placement, even as volume stays flat or falls, signal that the council is managing higher-need cases. This is not a volume problem that can be controlled; it is a complexity problem that raises costs regardless of headcount. Both NRPF and placements are statutory or near-statutory, limiting the council's ability to control spending.
findings.figures: Placement Support/Placements overspend £1.151m; actual placements 259 vs budget 275; External Residential 27 placements cost £14.564m vs budget £11.405m (variance £3.159m); Supported Accommodation 20 placements cost £1.574m vs budget £1.038m (variance £0.536m); NRPF overspend £0.707m
findings.quote: While the number of placements (259) remains below the budget assumption (275), costs are increasing due to greater complexity of need and higher support packages. In addition, ad hoc placement costs increase, reflecting higher overall placement activity, greater complexity of need, and increased unit costs, which together drive the financial pressure.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast to reach £42.530m by 2028/29, driven by exponential EHCP demand growth
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £5.302m in 2025/26 (2.94% of the £71.976m budget), with the High Needs Block alone accounting for £6.251m of that overspend. The council's DSG Management Plan forecasts the accumulated deficit will reach £42.530m by 2028/29 if current demand trends continue. The drivers are clear: total EHCPs/places funded by High Needs Block forecast to grow from 2,791 (2025/26) to 3,970 (2028/29), while High Needs expenditure is forecast to rise from £48.055m (2025/26) to £61.854m (2028/29), against assumed DSG funding rising only to £46.717m. Though the government announced a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the deficit up to end 2025/26, Thurrock must contribute the remaining 10% (£0.492m in 2025/26, £1.031m in 2026/27, £1.217m in 2027/28).
findings.matters: A spiralling DSG deficit is not discretionary spending — it is statutory SEND provision. A £42.5m accumulated deficit by 2028/29 signals fundamental mismatch between the council's SEND offer and its funding, and the government's stability grant covers only part of the problem for only three years. This creates ongoing structural pressure on the General Fund.
findings.figures: 2025/26 DSG overspend £5.302m; High Needs Block overspend £6.251m; Accumulated DSG deficit forecast: 2026/27 £4.919m, 2027/28 £15.226m, 2028/29 £42.530m; Thurrock's 10% contribution obligation £2.739m over 2025/26–2027/28
findings.quote: Officers continue to work with the Schools Forum to consider the financial challenges arising from the significant increase in demand for EHCP's and complexity of need; alongside the sufficiency of the local offer to prevent high-cost external placements. Current forecasts show that by the end of 2028/29 financial year, the deficit is projected to be £42.530m.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care has a £3.178m structural overspend that requires permanent solution from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care & Health directorate overspent by £3.178m in 2025/26, driven primarily by external placement costs (£1.659m), with particular pressures in Learning Disabilities (£0.576m from young people transitioning to adult services) and Mental Health (£0.863m from demand volatility). The council explicitly states that this is a structural deficit: unless addressed, it will 're-emerge and compound the challenge in future years' and the MTFS from 2027/28 will need to incorporate 'a permanent solution, whether through demand management, service transformation, additional funding, or savings'.
findings.matters: A structural budget gap that the council acknowledges cannot be managed through one-off mitigations signals ongoing spending pressure that will require either service cuts or additional funding — material risk for a lender assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: £3.178m overspend; External placements £1.659m (Older People £0.220m, Learning Disabilities £0.576m, Mental Health £0.863m); external placement demand driven by 'increased demand, complexity of need and higher placement costs'
findings.quote: Unless the structural budget gap is addressed, this pressure will re-emerge and compound the challenge in future years. From 2027/28 onwards, the Medium-Term Financial Strategy will therefore need to incorporate a permanent solution, whether through demand management, service transformation, additional funding, or savings, to ensure that the budget is brought back into a sustainable position.

findings.headline: Asset disposal and divestment programme, delivering £104.1m over three years, is critical to council's debt reduction strategy but faces market timing risk
findings.detail: In 2025/26 disposals achieved £18.822m against a revised budget of £16.840m. Divestments delivered £1.752m against a budget of £6.175m (shortfall attributed to timing differences). The council has reprofiled planned receipts totalling £104.1m to be realised by end of 2027/28. The report states explicitly that ongoing delivery "will be critical to reducing this reliance and improving the Council's long-term financial sustainability".
findings.matters: The council is betting on asset sales to reduce debt and improve sustainability. If market conditions worsen or key sales fail to close, the council will face either higher debt servicing costs or further need for EFS. This is a timing and market risk built into the forward plan.
findings.figures: 2025/26 disposals £18.822m (vs. £16.840m budget); divestments £1.752m (vs. £6.175m budget); total planned receipts £104.1m by end 2027/28; significant transactions estimated at £40m reprofiled to future years
findings.quote: Ongoing delivery of both programmes will be critical to reducing this reliance and improving the Council's long-term financial sustainability, with continued focus required on progressing transactions, managing delivery risks, and ensuring that future assumptions within the Medium Term Financial Strategy remain robust and achievable.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account repairs backlog presents medium-term risk despite current surplus position
findings.detail: HRA reported a £1.702m surplus transferred to reserves. However, repairs and maintenance overspent by £1.178m driven by backlog works, higher void costs, and compliance activity. The executive summary flags this explicitly: "underlying pressures in repairs continue to present medium-term risks". The HRA business plan is under separate review.
findings.matters: A backlog in housing repairs, even if funded this year via surplus drawdown, represents deferred maintenance and future liability. A council with constrained finances may find repairs backlogs grow. This matters to lenders because the housing stock is both a service asset and a potential security interest.
findings.figures: HRA repairs & maintenance overspend £1.178m against budget £14.643m; attributed to backlog works, voids, and compliance costs
findings.quote: Repairs & Maintenance: £1.178m overspend arising from backlog works, higher void costs, and increased compliance activity.

findings.headline: Capital programme severely slipped: £87.462m (73%) underspend against £120.250m budget
findings.detail: General Fund capital was budgeted at £120.250m and delivered £32.788m (27% of plan). Of this, £82.051m was slippage (schemes delayed into future years) and £5.411m was actual spend reduction. The slippage relates to procurement delays, planning requirements, and programme dependencies. A deep-dive review of capital slippage is flagged as a priority to understand future treatment.
findings.matters: 73% slippage is very high and signals either overambitious planning or poor delivery governance. While slippage technically does not worsen the year-to-year revenue position, it raises questions about the council's ability to execute its capital strategy and whether future-year forecasts are credible.
findings.figures: General Fund capital budget £120.250m; outturn £32.788m; underspend £87.462m (73%); slippage £82.051m; reduced spend £5.411m
findings.quote: The General Fund Capital programme reports an £87.462m underspend (73%) against a revised budget of £120.250m, of which £82.051m relates to slippage and £5.411m to reduced programme spend.

findings.headline: Treasury underspend of £10.104m, including £7.303m on commercial income, is non-recurring and masks underlying financing costs
findings.detail: The council realised £7.303m of favourable commercial income and £6.194m underspend on interest payable due to lower debt and improved cash balances. But the report states explicitly that "a proportion of these variances are non-recurring" and that "the MTFS will need to reflect underlying financing costs on a sustainable basis". These windfalls are not part of the structural operating position.
findings.matters: The £9.217m headline underspend largely evaporates when treasury one-offs are removed. This inflates the council's perceived financial position and makes the underlying deficit worse than the year-end picture suggests. Lenders need the recurring position.
findings.figures: Treasury underspend £10.104m; commercial income £7.303m (favourable); interest payable £6.194m (underspend); MRP pressure £3.394m (overspend). Subtotal of one-off factors exceeds total treasury underspend.
findings.quote: A proportion of these variances are non-recurring, and the MTFS will need to reflect underlying financing costs on a sustainable basis.

findings.headline: Council relies on unsustainable reserve drawdowns to absorb budget pressures, acknowledged as unfit for the medium term
findings.detail: General fund reserves now stand at £82.137m (including earmarked), increased by net £11.063m in-year through a combination of transfers and drawdowns. The council explicitly states this reliance "is not sustainable over the medium term" (section 15.4). The strategy is to manage short-term pressures while savings plans are delivered, but underlying demand and overspends in social care and education suggest reserves will continue to be drawn.
findings.matters: Reserves are a finite buffer. If used to cover recurring overspends in demand-led services rather than true one-offs, they will deplete predictably. A council that has signalled it will lean on reserves while solving deeper problems may find reserves inadequate faster than forecast.
findings.figures: General fund earmarked reserves £77.217m at 31 March 2026 (moved from £69.497m); general fund balance £11.000m; total £88.217m; net transfer to reserves in-year £11.063m
findings.quote: The use of reserves reflects the Council's planned approach to managing financial pressures in the short term. However, this reliance on reserves is not sustainable over the medium term.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspend of £5.302m, with cumulative deficit forecast to reach £42.530m by 2028/29
findings.detail: High Needs Block growth is the driver (£6.251m overspend alone). Independent and out-of-borough placements cost £2.0m over budget. The underlying structural problem is demand growth for EHCP support in both mainstream and specialist settings. Government proposals may cover up to 90% of the accumulated deficit, but this is subject to a SEND reform plan and is not yet assured.
findings.matters: A £42m cumulative deficit in a ringfenced fund presents a material and growing financial risk. If government support does not materialise as proposed, this deficit must be absorbed. The council describes this as a material financial risk requiring system reform and demand management.
findings.figures: £5.302m overspend 2025/26 (7.37% of £71.977m budget); High Needs Block £6.251m overspend; independent/out-of-borough placements £2.0m over; cumulative deficit forecast £42.530m by 2028/29
findings.quote: The DSG Management Plan forecasts a cumulative deficit of £42.530m by 2028/29, highlighting a significant structural funding gap driven by sustained demand growth.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspent by £3.178m and deteriorated a further £3.783m in Q4, with no permanent solution identified
findings.detail: External placements, provider services, and commissioning show persistent, demand-driven cost pressures. The position worsened significantly between Q3 and outturn, driven by transition cohorts, complex cases, and learning disabilities demand. The council states this is an ongoing cost pressure with implications for future financial sustainability, and is undertaking a deep-dive review. No permanent fix is planned before 2027/28.
findings.matters: Demand-led overspends that worsen in-year and have no permanent solution represent a rolling structural deficit in a major service. Lenders need to know whether this can be contained within future budgets or will consume further reserves and subsidies.
findings.figures: £3.178m overspend 2025/26 (budget £48.221m); deteriorated £3.783m since Q3; movements driven by "transition cohorts and an increase in complex, high-cost cases"
findings.quote: The outturn position has deteriorated by £3.783m since Quarter 3, reflecting emerging demand-led pressures, most evident within Learning Disabilities and Mental Health services, driven by transition cohorts and an increase in complex, high-cost cases.

findings.headline: Thurrock remains dependent on £59.070m annual exceptional financial support (capitalisation direction) to achieve a balanced budget
findings.detail: The council's operating budget requires annual government subsidy to balance. While the EFS requirement fell from £72.128m budgeted to £59.070m at outturn, this remains a massive and ongoing dependency. The council's own revenue operations do not cover its costs. This figure is provisional pending external audit.
findings.matters: A borrower dependent on annual government subsidy to function is fundamentally constrained in its capacity to service debt. The loan book is underpinned by subsidized funding, and any change in government support availability becomes a covenant risk.

findings.detail: The Council budgeted £6.175m in divestment receipts for 2025/26 but achieved only £1.752m. Most significantly, two wind farm disposals expected in late 2024/25 have slipped by a full year to 2026/27. These c£40m proceeds are central to reducing the Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.matters: Disposal slippage directly extends the period of government dependence and increases the risk that conditions for the £200m relief package cannot be met. Further slippage would materially worsen the financial outlook.

findings.headline: Interest rates rose above 6% versus forecast 4.80%, and 75% of debt is short-term, creating significant refinancing risk
findings.detail: Treasury advisors forecast longer-term PWLB rates would fall to 4.80%. Instead, geopolitical factors caused rates to rise above 6% in late 2025/26. With 75% of the debt portfolio in short-term funds, refinancing risk is high—a rate spike would immediately increase servicing costs and compress the already tight budget.
findings.matters: The council's debt costs are highly vulnerable to further rate increases. Actual rates diverging significantly from forecasts undermines the credibility of financial projections and shows real-time exposure to market conditions.

findings.headline: Council cannot balance its budget without ongoing exceptional government support; structural deficit driven by legacy debt costs
findings.detail: The annual deficit of £59.1m in 2025/26 is primarily composed of £52.2m in treasury management costs (debt interest and minimum revenue provision). Without the capitalisation direction from MHCLG, the council cannot operate a balanced budget. This is not a forecasting variance but a structural reality.
findings.matters: The deficit cannot be closed by service reductions or efficiency gains alone; it is entirely driven by legacy commercial investment debt. Financial sustainability requires either continued government support or massive asset sales.

findings.quote: This Council cannot currently operate a balanced budget without exceptional external support from the MHCLG through the annual capitalisation direction (CD). The budget deficit is primarily due to the treasury management costs (MRP and debt interest costs) associated with the historic commercial investment programme. In 2025/26 these £52.2m treasury management costs form the main part of the Council's estimated annual deficit (£59.1m)

The report explicitly notes that formal approval and implementation details have yet to be issued, creating uncertainty over both timing and whether conditions can be met.

findings.headline: PWE Holdings investment now represents 94% equity stake following refinancing
findings.detail: The council originally invested £30m in PWE Holdings bonds in 2018. Following refinancing and maturity, most debt was converted to equity, leaving the council as 94% owner of PWE with £2m debt still being repaid as a loan. This is a large, concentrated equity position in a private company.
findings.matters: The council has a large illiquid equity stake in a private company. This represents potential write-down risk and ties up capital that could otherwise be deployed to reduce borrowing.
findings.figures: Council owns 94% of PWE; £2m outstanding loan; originally invested £30m in bonds
findings.quote: The Council originally invested £30 m in bonds in PWE Holdings in three tranches in 2018. £20 m was outstanding when the bonds matured in December 2020. Following a refinancing the Council received a payment of £1m debt in 2022. The Council retained a debt of £2m which is being repaid as a loan, but the remainder of the debt was converted to equity making the Council the majority (94%) owner of PWE.

findings.headline: Overall opinion is LIMITED ASSURANCE, indicating material control risks
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive issued LIMITED ASSURANCE on the Council's framework of governance, risk management and internal control. The opinion reflects historic control weaknesses and findings from 2025/26 showing a significant number of instances where established controls were not consistently applied in practice.
findings.matters: Limited assurance signals that identified issues, if not addressed, significantly increase the likelihood of risks materialising and objectives not being met. This is a critical governance assessment for credit risk.
findings.figures: 1 audit received No Assurance, 11 received Limited Assurance, 8 received Reasonable Assurance out of 20 completed audits
findings.quote: This reflects the continued impact of historic control and governance weaknesses, together with findings from Internal Audit work in 2025/26 which identified a significant number of instances where established controls were not consistently applied in practice.

findings.headline: All new borrowing requires Commissioner approval, indicating ongoing external financial supervision
findings.detail: The council explicitly requires Commissioner approval for any new borrowing, with the capital refresh mentioning that 'any new borrowing requiring Commissioner approval'. The involvement of Commissioners as approvers of financial decisions indicates the council is under formal intervention or enhanced supervision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has autonomous decision-making authority. Commissioner oversight signals that the council is subject to external constraint and that decisions may be reversible or subject to external direction.
findings.figures: Commissioner approval required for new borrowing
findings.quote: reduced reliance on borrowing for the General Fund and for the HRA with any new borrowing requiring Commissioner approval

findings.headline: New governance controls and 'robust business case' requirement introduced for capital projects
findings.detail: The council is implementing new requirements for all capital projects, including mandatory Treasury Management compliance and robust business cases before funding is released. The Commissioner's comments note this is 'the first stage' of a governance framework that 'will need to evolve over time', indicating these are new controls in response to identified weaknesses.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess management quality and internal controls. New governance requirements, especially when introduced retroactively, typically indicate previous failures in project selection or financial management that could apply to any credit facility.
findings.figures: New governance requirements effective 2026/27
findings.quote: A robust business case is needed for all new capital projects. Release of funding and approval is contingent on the receipt of a robust business case, which is TM Treasury compliant

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account is moving to significant new borrowing (£5.563m in 2028/29) while drawing down £51m of reserves
findings.detail: HRA is planned to take external borrowing of £0.910m in 2027/28 rising to £5.563m in 2028/29. Over the same three years, HRA reserves are forecast to decline from £18.689m to £14.191m (total drawdown of £51.149m), while also using £21.068m from capital receipts. This combination suggests HRA is becoming cash-constrained.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council sustainability needs to understand HRA financial health. Rapid reserve depletion combined with rising borrowing suggests rents or external funding are insufficient to cover capital maintenance and debt service, which would eventually flow through to the general fund.
findings.figures: HRA External Borrowing 2028/29: £5.563m; HRA Reserves declining from £18.689m to £14.191m; Reserves drawdown total £51.149m over three years
findings.quote: Financing - Housing Revenue Account... External Borrowing... 0.000 0.910 5.563... Reserves 18.689 18.269 14.191

findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales are being diverted to debt repayment, not capital funding
findings.detail: The council had assumed capital receipts of £8.293m would fund capital projects, but has determined that all capital receipts from divestments and asset disposals must instead be applied to debt reduction. Switching any funding source to borrowing requires Commissioner approval, which constrains the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand debt trajectory. When a council prioritizes debt repayment over capital investment, it signals either debt stress or external pressure to deleverage. The requirement for Commissioner approval indicates the council is under external financial supervision.
findings.figures: £8.293m capital receipts (reduced to £7.844m after adjustments) redirected to debt reduction
findings.quote: all capital receipts received through divestments and asset disposals are to be applied to debt reduction. To switch the funding source from capital receipt to prudential borrowing requires Commissioner approval

findings.headline: £3 million borrowing requirement identified but approval deferred due to slippage concerns
findings.detail: The capital refresh identified a residual £3.003m of additional borrowing required for years 2027/28 and 2028/29. However, the council has explicitly declined to recommend approval of this borrowing because of the high slippage reported at Q3. This creates an unresolved funding gap that will need to be revisited.
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on future funding needs. A deferred-but-not-eliminated borrowing requirement signals unresolved financial pressure and suggests additional borrowing will eventually be required, but on uncertain timescales.
findings.figures: £3.003m additional borrowing required 2027/28-2028/29
findings.quote: At this stage the Council is not recommending that £3.003m of additional borrowing be agreed because of the high degree of slippage reported at quarter 3.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme has delivered only 48% of planned expenditure (52% underspend at Q3)
findings.detail: A significant underspend (£61.780m / 52%) was forecast against the Council's General Fund Capital Programme at quarter 3. The council has introduced a Capital Overview Board and new governance requirements specifically to address this slippage problem, indicating it is a longstanding delivery issue rather than a one-off.
findings.matters: A lender assessing whether the council can execute a capital investment plan needs to understand whether it can actually deliver. A 52% execution rate suggests either unrealistic planning, poor project management, or capability constraints that would apply to any new borrowing.
findings.figures: £61.780m / 52% underspend forecast at Q3 2025/26
findings.quote: At Quarter 3, a significant underspend (£61.780m / 52%) is forecast against the Council's General Fund Capital Programme.

findings.headline: Debt relief from MHCLG/HM Treasury ahead of Local Government Reorganisation is mentioned but not secured
findings.detail: The strategy references 'an element of debt relief to Thurrock ahead of local government reorganisation (LGR)' and relies on it to make the long-term position affordable. However, the amount, timing, and conditions are not stated—only that MHCLG/HM Treasury 'have committed'. This is a political decision, not a contractual obligation.
findings.matters: The entire 2027/29 forecast assumes debt relief that is not yet quantified or secured. If negotiations fail, or if LGR is delayed or cancelled, the council's path becomes unaffordable. This introduces significant political and timing risk.
findings.figures: MHCLG/HM Treasury committed to provide 'an element of debt relief' before LGR, but no figures or timeline stated
findings.quote: MHCLG /HM Treasury have committed to provide an element of debt relief to Thurrock ahead of local government reorganisation (LGR).

findings.headline: Divestment of £0.9bn failed commercial portfolio is critical to plan; execution risk marked AMBER
findings.detail: The entire recovery strategy depends on selling the council's commercial property portfolio (bought under failed investment initiative) to generate capital receipts that reduce debt. The strategy explicitly names this as an AMBER risk: 'may be lower or unpredictable in timings leading to higher costs'. Market conditions, buyer appetite, or valuations could deteriorate.
findings.matters: If divestment proceeds fall short or delay, the council cannot hit its CFR reduction targets and will need further government support or more rapid service cuts. The plan is built on an assumption about asset sales that the council itself judges as uncertain.
findings.figures: £0.9bn commercial investment portfolio; capital receipts forecast 2026/27 £7.8m, 2027/28 £10.7m, 2028/29 £4.1m
findings.quote: Divestment income flows – The Council's treasury management plans are impacted by the expected divestment programme to provide a borrowing need and budgetary costs – These flows may be lower or unpredictable in timings leading to higher costs.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing of £232m is temporary and unsustainable; council using reserves as emergency liquidity
findings.detail: The council is funding £232m of its borrowing need using cash from reserves and working capital rather than external loans. This is explicitly stated as a short-term measure that 'is not expected that this cash position can be sustained into the future'. The council is drawing down reserves to paper over the structural deficit.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite. Once depleted, the council will have no buffer and will be forced to cut services or increase external borrowing immediately. This means the 2028/29 position is more fragile than the CFR figures suggest.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing 2025/26 £232m, forecast to reduce to £102m by 2028/29; CFR exceeds external debt by £232m in 2026/27
findings.quote: At the Council it is not expected that this cash position can be sustained into the future and as a prudent measure the internal borrowing difference between the Council's overall borrowing need, the CFR, and its actual external debt has been reduced by assuming a higher level of external borrowing.

findings.headline: High refinancing risk: majority of £939m debt is short-dated and exposed to rate rises
findings.detail: The council holds £939m external debt forecast for 31/3/27, with a 'relatively short dated' maturity profile. The strategy explicitly notes this 'exhibits risk of an adverse increase in interest rates' and acknowledges that most of the current portfolio will face refinancing at uncertain rates. The council is deliberately maintaining short-term debt pending government debt relief, but this creates exposure if rates remain high.
findings.matters: If interest rates do not fall as forecast, Thurrock faces a cliff: short-term debt matures and must be refinanced at potentially higher rates, escalating annual debt service costs beyond the MTFP. The council has no capacity to absorb this shock.
findings.figures: Actual gross debt on 31/3/26 £846m, forecast 31/3/27 £939m, 31/3/29 £1,037m; debt interest 2026/27 £39.6m
findings.quote: The current debt portfolio structure is relatively short-dated, and exhibits risk of an adverse increase in interest rates which will expose the majority of the current portfolio to higher interest rates and debt management costs.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement rising to £1.139bn by 2028/29 despite recovery plan
findings.detail: The council's total indebtedness (CFR) is forecast to increase from £1.092bn (2025/26) to £1.139bn (2028/29), a rise of £47m. This happens because the annual capitalisation direction (£69-57m) accumulates faster than debt repayment (MRP and capital receipts). The accumulated CD balance is expected to reach £437m by 2028/29, locked into long-term cost.
findings.matters: The council is not deleveraging; it is accumulating more debt from the government's exceptional support mechanism. Each year of deficit spending creates another layer of permanent cost that must be serviced.
findings.quote: the amount of the annual CD is added to the Council's indebtedness (Capital Financing Requirement, CFR). This subsequently attracts further debt interest costs and MRP to the ongoing budget requirement creating further budgetary pressure. The current trajectory of this accumulating process is unaffordable in the future

findings.headline: Council balances budget only through £68.9m government capitalisation direction support
findings.detail: Thurrock cannot balance its operational budget without exceptional financial support from MHCLG/HM Treasury. The net operational deficit is £5.8m, covered entirely by government borrowing permission (capitalisation direction). This means the council is dependent on political agreement year-on-year to remain solvent.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's revenue position is structurally broken, not cyclically pressured. This is not a temporary tightness; it is a permanent dependency on government forbearance.
findings.figures: £5.8m net deficit between operational budget and core funding in 2026/27; £68.9m capitalisation direction support; £63.1m non-HRA treasury costs
findings.quote: The Council's predicament means the budget can only be balanced by Government EFS through the mechanism of the CD. This means the Council can borrow capital monies to balance the revenue budgetary deficit.

findings.headline: External debt of £846m with Capital Financing Requirement rising to £1.139bn by 2028/29
findings.detail: As of 31 March 2026, estimated external debt is £846m. The Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) is estimated at £1.092bn for 31/03/26, rising to £1.139bn by 31 March 2029. The council is using internal borrowing (cash reserves) of £0.232m at 31 March 2026 to offset some external borrowing need, but this provides limited headroom. The debt servicing costs (treasury costs) are forecast at £63.080m for 2026/27 and rising to £68.747m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: The absolute debt levels are high and rising. The council's debt servicing costs consume significant portions of its budget and are forecast to increase. Rising CFR indicates ongoing structural deficits being financed through borrowing rather than resolved through operational improvements.
findings.figures: External debt £846m (31/03/26), CFR £1.092bn (31/03/26) rising to £1.139bn (31/03/29); internal borrowing £0.232m; treasury costs 2026/27 £63.080m, 2028/29 £68.747m
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the council's estimated level of external debt is £846m. The Council's debt requirement (capital financing requirement) is estimated to be £1.092bn by the 31/03/26 increasing to £1.139m by the end of 2028/29.

findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset reduced retained business rates income by £14.4m in a single year
findings.detail: Fair Funding 2.0 has reset the business rates baseline that Thurrock can retain. Retained business rates fell from £60.428m in 2025/26 to £46.012m in 2026/27. This is a one-year cliff-edge decline driven by the removal of a £3.198m collection fund surplus used in 2025/26 plus an increase in the tariff Thurrock pays into the national pool as a result of the reset. Unlike other funding changes, this reduction is not phased over three years, creating a material income shock.
findings.matters: A sudden £14.4m reduction in a major revenue stream signals reduced financial flexibility and increases reliance on other funding sources. It demonstrates the volatility of the council's income base and vulnerability to policy changes beyond its control.
findings.figures: Business rates retention fell from £60.428m (2025/26) to £46.012m (2026/27); collection fund surplus removal £3.198m; change occurring in one year, not phased
findings.quote: The removal of the collection fund surplus of £3.198m that supported the 2025/26 budget, and the impact of the national business rates reset leading to an increase in the tariff that Thurrock Council pays into the national pool. This reduction occurs I one year and is not phased over three years.

findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit forecast to reach £46.1m by 2028/29, with the council ultimately responsible for 10% after statutory override ends
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) accumulated deficit is currently £6.459m and is forecast to grow to £46.091m by the end of 2028/29. The statutory override protecting councils from recording this as a real budget shortfall ends in March 2028. The government has announced it will cover up to 90% of the historic DSG deficit accumulated by 2026/27 through a High Needs Stability Grant, but the council will be responsible for the remaining 10% plus any deficits accrued in 2026/27 and 2027/28.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit represents a substantial future liability that could impact the council's financial sustainability. While the override provides temporary protection, the council may face a significant balance sheet hit in 2028 and responsibility for ongoing deficits in SEND spending that it cannot control.
findings.figures: 2025/26 accumulated deficit £6.459m, forecast 2028/29 deficit £46.091m; High Needs Block budget required £54.305m against allocation of £44.035m (£10.270m shortfall in 2026/27)
findings.quote: The accumulated deficit is forecast to grow by 2028/29 to an estimated at £46.091m. Whilst the statutory override remains in place, the deficit is held against the Council's reserves... the 10% remaining deficit will fall to local authorities to cover

findings.headline: Council cannot balance its budget without £68.9m exceptional financial support from central government
findings.detail: Thurrock requires an indicative Capitalisation Direction of £68.908m for 2026/27 to set a legally balanced budget. The council's core funding is £198.383m but its total budget requirement is £267.291m. Without this exceptional support, the council cannot meet its statutory obligation to set a balanced budget. This dependency has persisted for several years and is expected to continue through the medium term.
findings.matters: A council dependent on exceptional financial support to balance its budget presents material credit risk. The lender is effectively funding the gap between the council's revenues and its essential expenditures, with repayment uncertain.
findings.figures: Core funding £198.383m, Budget requirement £267.291m, EFS required £68.908m; total EFS requirement over seven years (2022/23-2028/29) is £637.574m, down from £691.280m forecast in February 2025
findings.quote: The Council's financial position remains exponentially challenging and will be so for several years with the Council requiring exceptional financial support (EFS), from central government, to achieve its legal requirement to set a balanced budget for the forthcoming year.
